title: Sweet shortcrust (pâte sucrée)
subtitle: The French-style sweet pastry for tarts, tartlets, and fruit bases
excerpt: Pâte sucrée is a sweet, rich shortcrust made with icing sugar, egg yolk, and a higher ratio of butter than standard shortcrust. It bakes to a firm, sandy, slightly biscuity base that holds without puffing or shrinking. It is the standard casing for lemon tart, fruit tarts, and chocolate tart.
sourceNotes: Pâte sucrée is a classic French patisserie base, documented across French baking tradition. The creaming method (crémage) with icing sugar is the standard professional technique for producing a fine, even crumb.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough for one 23 cm tart case
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the rolled-out case in the tin, unbaked, for up to 1 month. Blind bake from frozen, adding 5 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Wrap one disc and freeze.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be refrigerated for 3 days before use. The baked shell keeps in an airtight tin for 2 days.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven; fan 150°C, this pastry colours quickly so a lower temperature gives more control

glossaryTerms.definition: Pre-baking a pastry case without its filling, weighted down with baking paper and baking beans to prevent the base from puffing up.
The final smearing of pâte sucrée dough across the work surface with the heel of the hand. It distributes the butter evenly without developing gluten. The French term for this step.

content.text: Pâte sucrée is richer and more biscuity than standard shortcrust. The creaming method, beating butter and icing sugar before adding egg and flour, produces a finer, more tender crumb that holds its shape cleanly and resists the wet fillings of lemon curd and pastry cream.
180 g plain flour, 90 g unsalted butter (softened, not melted), 70 g icing sugar, 2 egg yolks, a pinch of salt. Some versions add 1 tbsp cold water if the dough is too dry.
Beat the softened butter and icing sugar together until pale and smooth. This is the creaming stage; it takes 2 to 3 minutes by hand.
Beat in the egg yolks one at a time. Add the salt.
Add the sifted flour all at once. Mix until it just comes together, a sandy, crumbly dough. Do not over-mix.
Tip the dough onto the bench and perform a
: smear the dough away from you with the heel of your hand in 3 or 4 strokes. Gather it back into a disc, wrap, and chill for at least 1 hour.
Lining the tin and blind baking

Roll cold on a lightly floured surface to 3 mm thickness. Line the tart tin, pressing gently into the corners. Trim the overhang. Prick the base lightly and chill for 20 minutes. Line with baking paper, fill with baking beans, and
at 170°C (conventional) for 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans and bake for a further 8 to 10 minutes, until pale gold and dry to the touch.
